summary: This is a domain class: a single blueprint that describes one product sold at a farmers' market, bundling its name, vendor, price, category, season, and whether it is organic. Later exercises in the chapter build streams over lists of these objects, so getting the shape of the data right first makes the stream code readable.

lines.text: Fields are `private` so no outside code can reach in and change them, and `final` so each value is fixed once the object is built. A class built this way is called immutable, and immutable objects are safe to use in streams.
`double` holds a decimal number, which is what a price needs. (For real money handling, production code prefers `BigDecimal`, but `double` keeps the stream examples uncluttered.)
A `boolean` field stores a simple yes-or-no fact, making it a natural target for stream filters later on.

lines.text: The constructor is the only way to create a `MarketProduct`, so every object exists fully populated from the moment it is born.
The parameter and the field share the name `name`, so `this.name` says "the field belonging to this object" while the bare `name` means the parameter.
A getter hands out a copy of the stored value without exposing the field itself. Streams call these methods through method references such as `MarketProduct::getName`.
By Java convention, getters for `boolean` values start with `is` rather than `get`, which makes conditions read like English.
This annotation tells the compiler you intend to replace a method inherited from `Object`. If you misspell the method name, compilation fails instead of silently doing nothing.
Overriding `toString` decides what a `MarketProduct` looks like when printed. Without it, `System.out.println` would show a meaningless class name and hash code.
The pieces are joined with `+` across several lines to build one readable line of output; the `'\''` entries are escaped single quotes that wrap the text values.
